stem: A company runs a web application in the us-east-1 Region and keeps a static maintenance page in an Amazon S3 bucket that is configured as a website. The company creates Amazon Route 53 failover records for www.example.com. The primary record is an alias record for an Application Load Balancer. The secondary record points to the S3 website endpoint. The company must ensure that Route 53 sends users to the maintenance page when the application cannot serve requests. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: The primary record is an alias record for an Application Load Balancer
when the application cannot serve requests

options.text: Create a Route 53 health check that sends HTTP requests to the primary endpoint, and associate the health check with the primary record.
options.why: It works, but AWS says to [associate health checks only with non-alias records](../facts/route53.md#route53-health-check-alias-record-not-recommended); this alias record can take its health from the load balancer.

options.text: Run a scheduled AWS Lambda function that tests the application every minute and repoints the primary record to the S3 website endpoint on failure.
options.why: It works, but it adds code to run and record edits, and AWS calls such edits [a non-statically-stable design](../facts/route53.md#route53-fi-record-edits-depend-on-control-plane).
options.misconception: Failover needs custom code that edits the records.

options.text: Turn on Evaluate Target Health for the primary record, so that Route 53 uses the health of the resource that the record points to.
options.why: For an alias record that points to an AWS resource such as a load balancer, you [set Evaluate Target Health to Yes](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-to-aws-use-evaluate-target-health-not-health-check) and create no health check.

options.text: Create a Route 53 health check of the S3 website endpoint, and associate the health check with the secondary record.
options.why: Route 53 [responds to DNS queries using the secondary record](../facts/route53.md#route53-failover-one-primary-one-secondary-responds-secondary-when-unhealthy) when the primary is unhealthy, so a check on the secondary does not detect the application failure.

explanation: Route 53 [responds to DNS queries using the primary record](../facts/route53.md#route53-failover-one-primary-one-secondary-responds-secondary-when-unhealthy) when the primary is healthy, so the primary needs a health signal. This primary is an alias record for a load balancer. Setting Evaluate Target Health lets Route 53 [route traffic away from unhealthy resources](../facts/route53.md#route53-evaluate-target-health-benefit-for-elb-beanstalk), with no health check to create or pay for.
takeaway: Failover primary that is an alias record for a load balancer: turn on Evaluate Target Health, not a separate health check.
twin: If the stem said "an A record with the Elastic IP address of one EC2 instance" instead: a Route 53 health check on the primary, because instances need a [record and a health check for each resource](../facts/route53.md#route53-simple-config-alias-targets-no-health-check-needed).
say: The primary is an alias record for a load balancer, so I'd turn on Evaluate Target Health and skip the extra health check.

stem: A company has a hybrid network. Its data center connects to a VPC in the eu-west-1 Region through an AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection. The VPC is associated with an Amazon Route 53 private hosted zone named corp.internal. DNS servers in the data center host the zone onprem.corp. Servers in the data center must resolve names in corp.internal. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Servers in the data center must resolve names in corp.internal

options.text: Create an outbound Resolver endpoint and a forwarding rule for onprem.corp that targets the data center DNS servers, and associate the rule with the VPC.
options.why: [Outbound Resolver endpoints allow DNS queries](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-outbound-endpoint-definition) from the VPC to the data center, which is the opposite direction: onprem.corp names for the VPC.

options.text: Run DNS forwarder software on EC2 instances in two Availability Zones, and configure both networks to forward queries for the other zone to them.
options.why: It works, but endpoints and rules forward queries [without having to deploy additional DNS servers](../facts/route53.md#route53-hybrid-resolver-endpoints-no-extra-dns-servers), so forwarder instances add patching and scaling work.
options.misconception: Hybrid DNS needs forwarder instances that the company runs.

options.text: Create an inbound Resolver endpoint in the VPC, and configure the data center DNS servers to forward corp.internal queries to the endpoint's IP addresses.
options.why: [Inbound Resolver endpoints allow DNS queries](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-inbound-endpoint-definition) into the VPC from the data center, so its DNS servers forward corp.internal queries to the endpoint.

options.text: Configure the data center DNS servers to forward corp.internal queries to the VPC Resolver address at the base of the VPC CIDR range plus two.
options.why: Forwarding from on-premises DNS servers to the CIDR+2 address [is not supported, and can cause unstable results](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-cidr-plus-two-forwarding-unsupported).

explanation: The queries start in the data center and need answers from the private hosted zone, so they travel into the VPC. Inbound endpoints carry queries [from your on-premises network or another VPC](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-inbound-endpoint-definition), and Route 53 VPC Resolver answers them from corp.internal. AWS names [conditional forwarding rules and Resolver endpoints](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-vpc-resolver-hybrid-forwarding-direct-connect-vpn) as the way to resolve names across Direct Connect.
takeaway: Data center asks the VPC: inbound endpoint. VPC asks the data center: outbound endpoint and a forwarding rule.
twin: If the stem said "EC2 instances in the VPC must resolve names in onprem.corp" instead: an outbound endpoint and a forwarding rule, because [Outbound Resolver endpoints allow DNS queries](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-outbound-endpoint-definition) out of the VPC.
say: The questions come from the data center into the VPC, so I'd create an inbound Resolver endpoint and forward corp.internal to it.

stem: A company hosts the DNS records for its domain, example.com, in an Amazon Route 53 public hosted zone. The company's website runs on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The marketing team wants users to open the website by typing example.com in a browser, without the www prefix. The DNS answer for example.com must keep working when the load balancer scales. Which DNS record should a solutions architect create in the hosted zone to meet these requirements?
keywords: must keep working when the load balancer scales

options.text: A CNAME record for example.com whose value is the DNS name of the Application Load Balancer.
options.why: The [DNS protocol does not allow you to create](../facts/route53.md#route53-cname-dns-protocol-forbids-zone-apex) a CNAME record at the zone apex, and example.com is the apex.

options.text: An alias record of type A for example.com that points to the Application Load Balancer.
options.why: Unlike a CNAME record, [you can create an alias record](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-allowed-at-zone-apex) at example.com, and [Route 53 detects changes in the resource on its own](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-follows-resource-ip-changes).

options.text: An A record for example.com whose value is the current IP addresses of the Application Load Balancer.
options.why: Elastic Load Balancing scales the load balancer and its DNS entry has a [time-to-live (TTL) of 60 seconds](../facts/route53.md#route53-elb-dns-entry-updated-ttl-60), so copied addresses go stale.

options.text: An NS record for example.com whose value is the DNS name of the Application Load Balancer.
options.why: An NS record [identifies the name servers for the hosted zone](../facts/route53.md#route53-ns-record-identifies-name-servers); it delegates a domain and does not point a name to a load balancer.
options.misconception: An NS record points a domain to the resource that serves the website.

explanation: The name example.com is the zone apex, [the top node of a DNS namespace](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-allowed-at-zone-apex). An alias record to a load balancer works [both for the root domain](../facts/route53.md#route53-elb-alias-record-for-root-and-subdomains) and for subdomains. Route 53 supports alias records for [three types of load balancers](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-apex-alias-elb-three-types), and the Application Load Balancer is one of them.
takeaway: At the zone apex, use an alias record for an AWS resource; a CNAME record fits subdomains such as www.
twin: If the stem said "users open www.example.com" instead: a CNAME record would also resolve, because the rule that blocks it applies [for the top node of a DNS namespace](../facts/route53.md#route53-cname-dns-protocol-forbids-zone-apex), not for subdomains.
say: Example.com is the zone apex, so I'd use an alias record for the load balancer, not a CNAME record.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the DNS record that meets these requirements.
I mark the constraints: the name is example.com without www, the target is an Application Load Balancer, and the answer must keep working when the load balancer scales.
Before I look at the options, I predict a CNAME record to the DNS name of the load balancer, because a CNAME record maps one name to another name.

I remove the A record with the current IP addresses, because the load balancer changes its addresses as it scales. I remove the NS record, because an NS record names the name servers of a hosted zone, not a website.

Between the CNAME record and the alias record the difference is where the record sits; the stem says example.com, with no www. My first idea breaks because example.com is the zone apex, where the DNS protocol does not allow a CNAME record.
Check: the alias record of type A sits at the zone apex, points to the load balancer and follows its address changes. Time: 90 seconds.

stem: A media company serves users around the world from Application Load Balancers in eu-west-1 and us-east-1. Because of distribution rights, the company uses Amazon Route 53 geolocation records: users in Europe go to eu-west-1, and users in North America go to us-east-1. Users in South America, and some users whose location cannot be identified, get no answer from DNS. These users must be served from us-east-1. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: some users whose location cannot be identified

options.text: Add a geolocation record for each remaining continent, and point each new continent record to the us-east-1 load balancer.
options.why: Geolocation maps addresses to places, and [some IP addresses aren't mapped to a location](../facts/route53.md#route53-geolocation-maps-ip-addresses-some-unmapped), so those users still get no answer.

options.text: Add a latency record with the same name that points to the us-east-1 load balancer, so that it answers when no geolocation record matches.
options.why: Route 53 keeps policies apart: [you can't create non-latency records](../facts/route53.md#route53-latency-no-non-latency-record-same-name-type) with the name and type of latency records, so the two kinds cannot share a name.

options.text: Add a geolocation record for each remaining continent and a record with the location Default, all pointing to the us-east-1 load balancer.
options.why: It works, but the Default record [handles both queries from unmapped IP addresses](../facts/route53.md#route53-geolocation-default-record-handles-unmapped) and unlisted places, so the continent records add work and change nothing.
options.misconception: Each place needs its own geolocation record even when a default record exists.

options.text: Add a geolocation record with the location Default that points to the us-east-1 load balancer, and keep the existing records.
options.why: One record with [a value of Default for Location](../facts/route53.md#route53-geolocation-recommend-one-default-record) covers places without a record and [IP addresses that Route 53 can't identify a location for](../facts/route53.md#route53-geolocation-recommend-one-default-record).

explanation: If you do not create a default record, Route 53 [returns a "no answer" response](../facts/route53.md#route53-geolocation-no-default-no-answer) for places without a geolocation record. One Default record catches each query that no continent or country record matches, also queries from unmapped addresses. The Europe and North America records stay, so the distribution rights still hold.
takeaway: Geolocation records need one Default record for places without a record and for unmapped addresses.
twin: If the stem said "send each user to the Region with the lowest latency" instead: replace them with latency records, which route to [the Region that provides the best latency](../facts/route53.md#route53-choose-latency-routing-best-latency-region).
say: Without a Default geolocation record some users get no answer, so I'd add one Default record for us-east-1.

stem: A company runs a web application behind an Application Load Balancer in us-east-1 and keeps a warm standby copy behind another Application Load Balancer in us-west-2. Amazon Route 53 hosts the company's public DNS records. The cross-Region recovery plan must move users to us-west-2 when the application in us-east-1 fails, even if the Route 53 control plane is impaired during the event. Which combination of steps will make the plan the MOST resilient? (Select TWO.)
keywords: even if the Route 53 control plane is impaired during the event

options.text: During the event, change the weights of weighted alias records so that the us-west-2 load balancer gets all the traffic.
options.why: It works only when the control plane works: [this is a control plane operation](../facts/route53.md#route53-dr-weight-change-is-control-plane), so it is less resilient.

options.text: Create failover alias records in advance, with the us-east-1 load balancer as the primary and the us-west-2 load balancer as the secondary.
options.why: AWS says to [pre-provision resources that require DNS records](../facts/route53.md#route53-fi-preprovision-for-multi-region-dr), so no record change is needed during the event.

options.text: During the event, create a new record that points the application's domain name to the us-west-2 load balancer.
options.why: Creating records to fail over is [a non-statically-stable design](../facts/route53.md#route53-fi-record-edits-depend-on-control-plane), because it depends on the control plane.

options.text: Base the health of the primary record on a health check or on Evaluate Target Health, so that Route 53 fails over by itself.
options.why: Health-based failover is a [highly reliable operation done on the data plane](../facts/route53.md#route53-dr-health-check-failover-data-plane), so no person must act during the event.

options.text: Before the event, move the hosted zone from us-east-1 to us-west-2 so that DNS changes can be made in us-west-2.
options.why: Public DNS, private DNS and health checks in Route 53 are [all global services](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-route53-still-global-service), so a hosted zone has no Region to move to.
options.misconception: A hosted zone lives in one Region and can move to another Region.

explanation: AWS says [you should not rely on the Route 53 control plane in your recovery path](../facts/route53.md#route53-fi-no-control-plane-in-recovery-path). In an impairment, DNS answers and health checks [will continue to work](../facts/route53.md#route53-fi-impairment-dns-and-health-checks-keep-working). So the records exist before the event, and health status moves the users.
takeaway: Create failover records before the event and let health status move users; record edits need the control plane.
twin: If the stem said "an operator must approve each failover" instead: change weights by hand, and accept that [this is a control plane operation](../facts/route53.md#route53-dr-weight-change-is-control-plane).
say: I'd create the failover records now and let health checks switch them, because editing records needs the control plane.

stem: A company runs a web application in the us-east-1 Region and keeps a static maintenance page in an Amazon S3 bucket that is configured as a website. The company creates Amazon Route 53 failover records for www.example.com. The primary record is an A record with the Elastic IP address of one EC2 instance. The secondary record points to the S3 website endpoint. The company must ensure that Route 53 sends users to the maintenance page when the application cannot serve requests. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: The primary record is an A record with the Elastic IP address of one EC2 instance
when the application cannot serve requests

options.text: Create a Route 53 health check that sends HTTP requests to the primary endpoint, and associate the health check with the primary record.
options.why: For resources without alias records, such as EC2 instances, you create a [record and a health check for each resource](../facts/route53.md#route53-simple-config-alias-targets-no-health-check-needed); a failing check moves users to the secondary.

options.text: Run a scheduled AWS Lambda function that tests the application every minute and repoints the primary record to the S3 website endpoint on failure.
options.why: It works, but it adds code to run and record edits, and AWS calls such edits [a non-statically-stable design](../facts/route53.md#route53-fi-record-edits-depend-on-control-plane).
options.misconception: Failover needs custom code that edits the records.

options.text: Turn on Evaluate Target Health for the primary record, so that Route 53 uses the health of the resource that the record points to.
options.why: Evaluate Target Health decides [whether Route 53 checks the health of the resource](../facts/route53.md#route53-evaluate-target-health-other-policies-checks-resource) that an alias record refers to; this A record is not an alias record.

options.text: Create a Route 53 health check of the S3 website endpoint, and associate the health check with the secondary record.
options.why: Route 53 [responds to DNS queries using the secondary record](../facts/route53.md#route53-failover-one-primary-one-secondary-responds-secondary-when-unhealthy) when the primary is unhealthy, so a check on the secondary does not detect the application failure.

explanation: Route 53 [responds to DNS queries using the primary record](../facts/route53.md#route53-failover-one-primary-one-secondary-responds-secondary-when-unhealthy) when the primary is healthy, so the primary needs a health signal. An A record with an Elastic IP address names no AWS resource whose health Route 53 can read. A Route 53 health check of the instance gives that signal, and a failing check sends users to the S3 maintenance page.
takeaway: A failover primary that points to an EC2 instance needs its own Route 53 health check.
twin: If the stem said "an alias record for an Application Load Balancer" instead: turn on Evaluate Target Health, because for that alias record you [set Evaluate Target Health to Yes](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-to-aws-use-evaluate-target-health-not-health-check).
say: The primary is a plain A record for one instance, so I'd attach a Route 53 health check to the primary record.

stem: A company has a hybrid network. Its data center connects to a VPC in the eu-west-1 Region through an AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection. The VPC is associated with an Amazon Route 53 private hosted zone named corp.internal. DNS servers in the data center host the zone onprem.corp. EC2 instances in the VPC must resolve names in onprem.corp. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: EC2 instances in the VPC must resolve names in onprem.corp
DNS servers in the data center host the zone onprem.corp

options.text: Create an outbound Resolver endpoint and a forwarding rule for onprem.corp that targets the data center DNS servers, and associate the rule with the VPC.
options.why: [Outbound Resolver endpoints allow DNS queries](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-outbound-endpoint-definition) from the VPC to the data center, and the forwarding rule sends onprem.corp names to the data center DNS servers.

options.text: Run DNS forwarder software on EC2 instances in two Availability Zones, and configure both networks to forward queries for the other zone to them.
options.why: It works, but endpoints and rules forward queries [without having to deploy additional DNS servers](../facts/route53.md#route53-hybrid-resolver-endpoints-no-extra-dns-servers), so forwarder instances add patching and scaling work.
options.misconception: Hybrid DNS needs forwarder instances that the company runs.

options.text: Create an inbound Resolver endpoint in the VPC, and configure the data center DNS servers to forward corp.internal queries to the endpoint's IP addresses.
options.why: [Inbound Resolver endpoints allow DNS queries](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-inbound-endpoint-definition) into the VPC from the data center, which is the opposite direction: corp.internal names for the data center.

options.text: Configure the data center DNS servers to forward corp.internal queries to the VPC Resolver address at the base of the VPC CIDR range plus two.
options.why: It serves corp.internal, not onprem.corp, and forwarding to the CIDR+2 address [is not supported, and can cause unstable results](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-cidr-plus-two-forwarding-unsupported).

explanation: The queries start in the VPC and need answers from the data center DNS servers, so they travel out of the VPC. Outbound endpoints carry queries [from your VPC to your on-premises network](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-outbound-endpoint-definition). Resolver rules decide which queries go out and [which queries VPC Resolver answers itself](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-rules-control-forwarding), so a rule for onprem.corp sends only those names.
takeaway: VPC asks the data center: outbound endpoint and a forwarding rule. Data center asks the VPC: inbound endpoint.
twin: If the stem said "Servers in the data center must resolve names in corp.internal" instead: an inbound endpoint, because [Inbound Resolver endpoints allow DNS queries](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-inbound-endpoint-definition) into the VPC.
say: The questions go from the VPC to the data center, so I'd create an outbound Resolver endpoint with a forwarding rule for onprem.corp.

stem: A company serves its website at the edge through an Amazon CloudFront distribution. IPv6 is turned on for the distribution, and example.com is an alternate domain name of the distribution. The company hosts example.com in an Amazon Route 53 public hosted zone. Users on IPv4 networks and users on IPv6 networks must reach the website at example.com. Which combination of actions should the company take in the hosted zone to meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: IPv6 is turned on for the distribution
Users on IPv4 networks and users on IPv6 networks

options.text: Create a CNAME record for example.com whose value is the domain name of the CloudFront distribution.
options.why: The [DNS protocol does not allow you to create](../facts/route53.md#route53-cname-dns-protocol-forbids-zone-apex) a CNAME record at the zone apex, and example.com is the apex.

options.text: Create an alias record of type A for example.com that points to the domain name of the CloudFront distribution.
options.why: With IPv6 turned on, you [create two records](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-cloudfront-ipv6-two-records) for the distribution; this alias record of type A answers the IPv4 users.

options.text: Create an A record for example.com that lists the IP addresses that the distribution's domain name returns today.
options.why: CloudFront addresses [vary based on your end user’s location](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-cloudfront-ip-addresses-vary-by-location) and can change, so a fixed list sends users to wrong edges.
options.misconception: CloudFront edge addresses stay fixed, so copied addresses keep working.

options.text: Create a Lambda function that rewrites A and AAAA records for example.com with the distribution's addresses every minute.
options.why: It adds code to run, and it copies addresses that [vary based on your end user’s location](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-cloudfront-ip-addresses-vary-by-location); alias records need no upkeep.
options.misconception: A script can keep copied CloudFront addresses current.

options.text: Create an alias record of type AAAA for example.com that points to the domain name of the CloudFront distribution.
options.why: An AAAA record routes traffic [using an IPv6 address](../facts/route53.md#route53-aaaa-record-ipv6), so this alias record serves the IPv6 users of the distribution.

explanation: Example.com is the zone apex, and an alias record can map it to [your Amazon CloudFront distribution](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-apex-alias-cloudfront). With IPv6 turned on, you [create two records](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-cloudfront-ipv6-two-records): type A for IPv4 and type AAAA for IPv6.
takeaway: Apex of a CloudFront site with IPv6: two alias records, type A and type AAAA.
twin: If the stem said "IPv6 is turned off for the distribution" instead: the alias record of type A is enough, because the AAAA record routes [using an IPv6 address](../facts/route53.md#route53-aaaa-record-ipv6).
say: For example.com on CloudFront with IPv6, I'd create two alias records, one of type A and one of type AAAA.

stem: A company runs its own DNS servers for its public domain on two Amazon EC2 instances in one Availability Zone of the us-east-1 Region. The DNS servers answer queries from customers on the internet. The company wants a fully managed DNS service that keeps answering queries if an Availability Zone or a whole AWS Region fails. What should a solutions architect recommend?
keywords: if an Availability Zone or a whole AWS Region fails

options.text: Move the DNS servers to EC2 instances in two Availability Zones of us-east-1, behind a Network Load Balancer.
options.why: Two Availability Zones survive a zone failure, but every server still sits in us-east-1, and the company still runs the DNS software itself.

options.text: Create a Route 53 private hosted zone for the domain, and associate it with VPCs in two AWS Regions.
options.why: A private hosted zone will [only return these records when queried from within](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-private-zone-answers-only-from-associated-vpcs) the associated VPCs, so internet customers get no answers.

options.text: Create inbound Resolver endpoints in two Availability Zones of us-east-1, and send the internet DNS queries to the endpoint addresses.
options.why: [VPC Resolver is a Regional service](../facts/route53.md#route53-vpc-resolver-regional) that answers queries that reach a VPC; it does not host a public domain for internet users.
options.misconception: Resolver endpoints serve a public domain to users on the internet.

options.text: Create a Route 53 public hosted zone for the domain, and update the domain's name servers at the registrar.
options.why: Route 53 offers [highly available and scalable Domain Name System (DNS)](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-what-is-route53-dns-domains-health) as a managed service, and its public DNS is not tied to one Region.

explanation: Public and private DNS in Route 53 are [all global services](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-route53-still-global-service), answered by a [global anycast network of DNS servers](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-global-anycast-low-latency). The loss of one zone or one Region does not stop the answers. The registrar has to use the zone's name servers, or Route 53 [will not be authoritative for queries](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-registrar-must-use-hosted-zone-name-servers).
takeaway: Public DNS that survives a zone or Region failure: a Route 53 public hosted zone.
twin: If the stem said "names that only instances in its VPCs resolve" instead: a private hosted zone, which will [only return these records when queried from within](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-private-zone-answers-only-from-associated-vpcs) associated VPCs.
say: Route 53 is a global managed DNS service, so I'd move the public zone there and update the name servers.

stem: A company registered the domain example.com with a third-party registrar, which also hosts the DNS records today. The company wants to migrate the DNS service for example.com to Amazon Route 53. Because of a contract, the domain registration must stay with the current registrar. Users on the internet must keep resolving the company's website during the change. What should the company do?
keywords: the domain registration must stay with the current registrar

options.text: Transfer the domain registration to Route 53 first, then create the records in the hosted zone that Route 53 creates for the domain.
options.why: A transfer is possible, but [this isn't required to use other Route 53 features](../facts/route53.md#route53-domain-transfer-not-required-for-other-features), and the contract keeps the registration where it is.

options.text: Create a Route 53 private hosted zone with the records, and associate the hosted zone with the VPC that runs the website.
options.why: A private hosted zone will [only return these records when queried from within](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-private-zone-answers-only-from-associated-vpcs) associated VPCs, so internet users get no answers.

options.text: Create a Route 53 public hosted zone with the records, then change the domain's name servers at the registrar to the hosted zone's name servers.
options.why: When another registrar manages the domain, you [update the name servers for your domain](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-external-registrar-must-update-name-servers) to the ones of the hosted zone, and Route 53 starts to answer.

options.text: Create the records in Route 53, and add a CNAME record at the registrar that points example.com to a Route 53 name server.
options.why: The [DNS protocol does not allow you to create](../facts/route53.md#route53-cname-dns-protocol-forbids-zone-apex) a CNAME record at example.com, and delegation names name servers, not a CNAME target.
options.misconception: A CNAME record at the registrar hands a domain to another DNS service.

explanation: If the registrar does not use the name servers of the hosted zone, Route 53 [will not be authoritative for queries](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-registrar-must-use-hosted-zone-name-servers) to the domain. So the company copies the records into a public hosted zone first, and then changes the name servers at the current registrar. A transfer of the registration is optional.
takeaway: Keep the registrar, move the DNS: create a public hosted zone and change the name servers at the registrar.
twin: If the stem said "the company also wants Route 53 as its registrar" instead: transfer the registration too, because [you can transfer the domain registration to Route 53](../facts/route53.md#route53-domain-transfer-not-required-for-other-features).
say: The registration can stay where it is; I'd create a public hosted zone and change the name servers at the registrar.

stem: A small team runs version 1 of a web application behind one Application Load Balancer. The team deploys version 2 behind a second Application Load Balancer in the same Region. The team wants about 10 percent of users to reach version 2 first, a larger share during the next week, and a quick way to send every user back to version 1 if errors appear. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: about 10 percent of users to reach version 2 first
send every user back to version 1

options.text: Create failover alias records with the version 1 load balancer as the primary and the version 2 load balancer as the secondary.
options.why: Route 53 answers with the secondary [when the first one is unhealthy](../facts/route53.md#route53-failover-routing-primary-or-secondary), so version 2 gets no users when version 1 works.
options.misconception: Failover records split traffic between two healthy versions.

options.text: Create weighted alias records for the two load balancers with weights of 90 and 10, and change the weights to shift users or roll back.
options.why: Route 53 answers in the [ratio of a resource's weight to the total](../facts/route53.md#route53-weighted-ratio-of-weight-to-total), and you [change the weight for that record to 0](../facts/route53.md#route53-weighted-routing-weight-zero-stops-traffic) to roll back.

options.text: Create multivalue answer alias records for the two load balancers, and change how many records each version has to shift users.
options.why: Multivalue answer alias records are [not supported](../facts/route53.md#route53-multivalue-alias-not-supported) in Route 53, so the load balancers cannot be targets of this routing policy.
options.misconception: Multivalue answer records can point to load balancers and split users by share.

options.text: Run a scheduled script that switches a simple alias record between the two load balancers to approximate the share of users.
options.why: It needs code, a schedule and monitoring, but weighted routing sends traffic to [multiple resources in proportions that you specify](../facts/route53.md#route53-choose-weighted-routing-proportions) without them.
options.misconception: Route 53 has no built-in way to split users by share.

explanation: AWS names weighted routing for [testing new versions of software](../facts/route53.md#route53-choose-weighted-routing-proportions). Route 53 answers each record in the ratio of its weight to the total, so weights of 90 and 10 send about one user in ten to version 2. A higher version 2 weight shifts more users, and a weight of zero on version 2 sends everyone back.
takeaway: Share users between versions with weighted records; a weight of zero takes one version out.
twin: If the stem said "version 2 receives users only when version 1 fails" instead: failover alias records, because the secondary answers [when the first one is unhealthy](../facts/route53.md#route53-failover-routing-primary-or-secondary).
say: I'd use weighted alias records at ninety and ten, raise version two over the week, and set it to zero to roll back.
